decisions.reason: With the target original resolved to Van Wermeskerken & Van Gog (2017), the authors state an explicit overall verdict that they replicated their previous findings: seeing the model's face reduced relative dwell time on the task area without affecting performance on either the molecule-building test or the knowledge test. Because both the attentional effect and the null learning effect match the findings of Van Wermeskerken & Van Gog (2017), the replication outcome is successful, whereas shipped 'mixed' reflected either a misreading of the null learning effect or comparison against the wrong chain source (Van Gog et al., 2014).

decisions.quote:
We first addressed our research question of whether TD adolescents'
performance on the molecule building task was affected when learning
from video modeling examples in which the model's face was either
visible or not visible. Mann–Whitney U tests did not reveal any
differences between the Face Visible and Face Not Visible conditions
(first build: U = 96.00, z = −0.607, p = .544, r = .11; second build:
U = 100.50, z = −0.420, p = .674, r = .08).

We first addressed our research question of whether TD adolescents'
performance on the molecule building task was affected when learning
from video modeling examples in which the model's face was either

(first build: U = 96.00, z = −0.607, p = .544, r = .11; second build:
U = 100.50, z = −0.420, p = .674, r = .08).
expert_decision.reason: van Wermeskerken, Luteijn, & van Gog (2022, 10.1016/j.actpsy.2022.103667) examine whether seeing the model's face in video modeling examples of a glutamine molecule-building task affects task performance among typically developing (TD) and ASD prevocational adolescents. The shipped row (input_row_index 237) is Van Gog, Verveer, & Verveer (2014, 10.1016/j.compedu.2013.12.004), an adult study using a 15-step puzzle task that found a positive effect of face visibility on the second learning attempt. By contrast, Van Wermeskerken & Van Gog (2017, 'Seeing the instructor's face and gaze in demonstration video examples affects attention allocation but not learning', Computers & Education, 113, 98–107, DOI 10.1016/j.compedu.2017.05.013) introduced the glutamine molecule-building video modeling task and 20-item knowledge test (adopted directly in the 2022 study's Method, lines 494–499 and 668–677) and found no effect of face visibility on learning performance. The 2022 paper frames its research question against both prior studies (lines 382–388) and explicitly states in the Discussion (lines 1072–1077): 'Consequently, our findings fail to replicate the study by Van Gog et al. (2014), who found a positive effect on learning on the second test task after watching the video for a second time, and replicate the findings by Van Wermeskerken and Van Gog (2017) as well as Van Wermeskerken et al. (2018), who did not find any beneficial or detrimental effects of visibility of the model's face in adult learners.' Van Wermeskerken & Van Gog (2017) is an independent primary empirical study missing from the shipped dataset. The prior state file (d707242d...json) recorded only a schema formatting error ('invalid decision or quote: type') from an earlier automated run, and no prior adjudication file exists.
